utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. If I could remind you, General, of the affirmation you took at the commencement of your evidence, which still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: General Pringle, in your view, is it likely that a battalion commander, on his own initiative -- well, let me back up for a second. If a favourable command climate is established, is it likely that a unit commander, at the battalion level, would conduct, on his own initiative, an operation, such as an attack, which is contrary to his commander's intent? Now, before you engage in an answer, can you explain the concept of commander's intent?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the commander's intent refers to -- well, exactly what it says, the intention of the commander, what the commander wants to achieve, what the commander has set the mission as, and the why. The what and the why make up the commander's intent. Your question is: Is it likely that a unit commander would carry out an action that was -- on his own initiative which was contrary to the commander's intent? Well, if he did, he would be knowingly carrying out an action that did not fit with his commander's intentions. That would not be a wise thing to do, for a number of reasons. First of all, it may throw the overall plan off course; secondly, he may not have the necessary combat and logistic support necessary to support his actions or to assist with, for example, ammunition resupply or casualty evacuation. So the short answer to your question: Would a unit commander be likely to carry out a deliberate attack which he knew would be contrary to his commander's intent? My answer to that is: That is highly unlikely, unless there's been an absolute breakdown in discipline.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How does a commander communicate his intent?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: A commander's intent is communicated through the order system, and that is, through a combination of written orders and verbal orders and the follow-up interaction between commanders at all levels that we were talking about yesterday. The first paragraph in an operational order is the situation, which would include the commander's -- different nations call it different things, but concept of operations or scheme of manoeuvre, which includes his intend, and that is where the commander lays down what it is he's trying to achieve and why, so that everybody can understand the part they have to play in it. The orders would then go on to allocate the mission. So that's the written and formal means of communicating intent. That would then be backed up by verbal instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If, as you suggested, the need for support, such as ammunition and the ability to take care of casualties were in place under the scenario described, that is, a unit, a battalion-level unit commander undertaking an operation supposedly at his own initiative. Are you able to indicate what that might suggest about commander's intent, if they were available and in fact used?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's differentiate a number of things here. First of all, the hypothetical unit in question that we're discussing might have its own integral combat support and logistics support. That combat and logistics support would be under the command and available to the unit commander in question. So the use of those assets is within the bailiwick of that commander and would not really indicate any more than that commander has decided to use them. But if assets outside the immediate command of that unit commander have been allocated and/or used, such as, for example, extra artillery or heavy mortars or helicopter support or logistics support, then that would indicate to me that there is more to the action described than simply a unit commander making his own decision in isolation and doing something. It would mean that there has been high-level coordination and assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: General, by assets outside the immediate command, would that include, then, other units in the area, the assistance from other units in the area?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would, if that assistance is pre-planned and those units have been notified that the unit planning an attack is going to attack at a certain time and other units have been put on standby to be ready to assist. That would be a sure indicator that there is more to this attack than simply the unit commander's personal decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And if the assistance, for the sake of argument, were not pre-planned but made available and continued to be made available, what, then, is the implication?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would mean -- that would indicate to me that the unit commander was acting within the instructions and the intent that he had previously received and that, in doing so, as would be normal, the rest of the operational forces are available for assistance, and indeed would be required to assist as necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: General, in your view, under what circumstances would that battalion commander risk undertaking an attack or an action which is contrary to his commander's intent, given the philosophy of, let's say, an army that is more orders-driven, centralist?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a commander that decides to conduct a deliberate, pre-planned attack which he knew was absolutely contrary to his commander's intent would be operating way outside his own authority. He would be operating in opposition to his commander's intent. He would be putting at risk the mission passed down by the commander. He would, in short, be seriously putting his neck on the line. And I say "deliberate attack" because there might be circumstances where a commander saw an opportunity to achieve the objective that he knew was within the commander's intent, and the opportunity suddenly presented itself, and the opportunity to use his initiative and achieve that objective suddenly presented itself, then he might do it. But that's not what we're talking about here, because your question is: If this was contrary to the commander's intent. If it's contrary to the commander's intent, actually, that commander -- well, in any disciplined army, would be liable for court-martial and dismissal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What would be your view, General, of the command climate and of the commander's intent where, in that commander's area of responsibility, on multiple occasions in a relatively short period of time, say several months, units under his control attacked sites which were protected both under international law and by specific standing orders?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here we're beginning to touch on what we were talking about yesterday. If specific standing orders have been given that these sorts of sites should be protected, not harmed, and not engaged, and yet they are being engaged, well, that is contrary to the orders given and the intent explained, and therefore, one would expect action to be taken to prevent that. At the very least, one would take -- one would consider, after it happened the first time, that an inquiry would be initiated as to find out why, and unless there was very, very good reason, disciplinary action at the appropriate level would follow. But if that's not happening, what we're beginning to say about the command climate is that these sorts of actions are acceptable, although we talked about window dressing yesterday. Although orders have been passed down the chain that these sorts of targets should not be engaged, the fact that nothing happens when they are engaged indicates to those that have been engaging them that this is perfectly acceptable and fair play. So either the commander's authority has been completely eroded, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and you talked about over a fairly lengthy period of time, and that's unlikely, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. I did say in a relatively short period of time.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I thought you said three months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for interrupting, but I have to ask a question which seems of great importance to me. I fail to understand the mimicry of the distinguished Madam Prosecutor. It is obvious what she is talking about here, it is obvious what she is driving at when she is asking the questions of the type that she has been asking. I think that it would be a fair way to proceed in this matter if she is already talking about these matters that you will be deciding upon at the end of these proceedings, I think it would be very fair to present to the distinguished witness what is it that she is talking about to present to him documents, to present evidence on which this is based, without any concealment, without any commonplace matters about specific things that we're talking about. The witness could give his opinion. He could look at the evidence. Namely, he could look at the written documents, he could look at the other evidence which is before him, and then render his opinion. Although I do believe that this is the opinion to be rendered by the panel, by the Court. I believe that madam Somers is presenting her case in detail except for the actual name. Why doesn't she say the name, the commander of the battalion, the commander whom she means, all the names that she means, and then we can talk about it. Actually, she has been doing this all the while, but in a disguised manner. Why? She wants to turn into -- a specific instance into a general situation before a gentleman who is a witness and rendering his views from the standpoint of the military profession. He has not been invited here to give his judgement on the specific situation, specific events. But if that is the case, let's present the evidence. Let Mr. Pringle say what he thinks happened on the 6th of December, what was Commander Kovacevic, Commander Strugar, Commander Jokic like, what was the command like, and then we can go about it and talk about it in this way. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that the line of questioning is entirely appropriate. We are asking questions directed at issues concerning command. It can be any scenario that would address the central issues of command. If it is more focussed to give at least some guidance for related types of circumstances, but I find it unnecessary to get into the orders, facts, et cetera, et cetera. We are looking at how a commander acts, behaves, communicates, and obligations, and that is the subject of inquiry, through climate, and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. As I understand the course being pursued by Ms. Somers, Mr. Petrovic, she is putting to the witness hypothetical situations. The witness is then giving his opinion of what would be the cause and effects in an ordinary military situation, drawing on his experience, set against the hypothetical position that is posed to him by Ms. Somers. That evidence may or may not prove useful to the Chamber when it comes to decide the case eventually. That will depend on whether other evidence has shown that there existed the same or a similar state of affairs as that which is being put hypothetically to the witness. If the other evidence doesn't match up and demonstrate that that situation actually existed, well, then the evidence of the witness may be of little or no use to the Chamber. But Ms. Somers is proceeding on the basis that she will, by other evidence, demonstrate that the hypothetical situation upon which the witness is being asked to express an opinion did in fact exist, and it's on that basis that I understand it that Ms. Somers is proceeding and that the witness is expressing his views. He is certainly not purporting to express an opinion on what was the situation in the JNA on the 6th of December, 1991, and if he were purporting to do that, there would be very serious issues about the admissibility and propriety of expert opinion on that, because as you did indicate that is a matter for this Chamber to decide, in light of all the evidence. So I think Ms. Somers is very properly avoiding taking that step, and we are merely being offered hypothetical evidence, the value of which will depend upon the other evidence led from the factual witnesses who can speak of the situation at the time. On that basis, we would certainly allow the present line of questioning to continue. Thank you. Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: General, if an attack on a protected site occurred during an attack on a military objective, what emergency measures should the higher command -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm reminded by my colleague that the last answer was interrupted. If I could just return to the question. I'm terribly sorry if this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No. I think the poor witness will have lost the thread of that anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. I have to go back on the other computer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. General, you had said I think a longer period, and I simply reminded you of the question, which indicated a relatively short period of time. Several months was my reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I say you might need to remind the Chamber of the question, as well as the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The whole question was: What would your view, General, be of the command climate and of the commander's intent where, in that commander's area of responsibility, on multiple occasions, in a relatively short period of time, say several months, units under his control attacked sites which were protected both under international law and by specific standing orders?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If, over several months, and contrary to standing orders, such sites had been attacked, then it would indicate to me, if no action had been taken about that, despite the fact that it was against standing orders, it would indicate to me that the command climate in which the units and formations are operating is one where, whilst orders are being passed concerning the sensitivity of various forms of actions and indeed the prohibition of various forms of actions, when those actions willy-nilly occur and nothing -- no disciplinary action follows, then that indicates -- that would indicate to the troops involved that those are quite acceptable actions, and the more often it happens without disciplinary action, the more that notion would be confirmed in their mind. They might ask themselves the question: Well, why are we being told that such actions are prohibited, and yet nothing is being done when we take those actions? We can only assume that there is some other reason for telling us, but actually, it's perfectly okay to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That was, I presume, as to command climate. And the second part of the question is: What would be your view of commander's intent under those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah. Well, if no action is taken up the disciplinary chain of command, one -- or I would draw the conclusion that, despite what is being written and ordered formally, actually, these actions lie well within commander's intent and what the commander finds acceptable, simply because if he didn't find it acceptable, he'd do something about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What additional measures, General, might you view as appropriate if a strategic-level order is passed down, let's say concerning a political meeting, a ceasefire. You can select the event, but one that would have significant strategic implications in the area of responsibility. What measures might be appropriate for the higher Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. commander to take concerning allowing escalation of hostilities immediately prior to the implementation of that either ceasefire or political action? But let's say for the sake of argument ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Let's take, for the sake of argument, a strategic event like an upcoming ceasefire arranged at high level. Now, this would be of particular significance to the higher-level commanders operating at that operational level, at the operational strategic interface. It would be of particular significance to that level of command. Therefore, I would expect commanders at that level to start taking the necessary actions to ensure that those that they command realise what is about to happen, realise how that might change orders previously given. I mean, if we're heading for a ceasefire and up until now we've been on the attack, that requires a change of order and a change of intent, I would suggest. And it puts a serious onus on the operational-level commander to make sure that the appropriate orders are passed down the chain. His subordinate commanders understand exactly what is going on, his subordinate commanders understand what they've got to do, and in particular, what changes to current procedures they should effect in order that nothing happens to knock off course the, in this case, the upcoming ceasefire, because the operational-level commander will realise that these are delicate situations and a tactical-level action can have strategic consequences if that tactical-level action is contrary to the direction in which he wants his command to be going. And so, in summary, an event like that would particularly focus the mind of the operational high-level commander, particularly focus his mind, because it will be his responsibility to make sure that it comes about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You just mentioned the phrase "so that nothing happens." Now, what, in your view, would have to be in the mind of a higher-level commander when you talk about "nothing happens"? What types of eventualities and how would he determine the span of measures necessary so that nothing happens? What would he take in mind to consider that and implement that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the high-level commander who, by definition, has experience, would realise that seeing conditions through to the successful implementation of this ceasefire is not necessarily going to be easy, because his troops are in contact -- well, let's assume his troops are in contact with the enemy. Let's assume his troops have been fighting the enemy for a period of months. Let's put it in the same context as the last question. So for a period of months, there have been exchanges of fire, there's been exchanges of artillery, exchanges of mortar fire, there have been attacks and counter-attacks, there have been wounded taken, there have been heavy resupply problems, there have been -- a lot of action has been taken, even if the front line may not have moved that much. Now, he will realise that if he is now tasked to move to effect a ceasefire, he's somehow got to stabilise the front and disengage, in order that neither side creates the conditions where a ceasefire simply can't come about. I mean, nobody is going to agree to the ceasefire starting at X-hundred hours when they're heavily engaged attacking each other and artillery and mortar is falling on all these positions. And that's -- those are the conditions that he's got to avoid. So he's got to now start taking positive action, issuing orders, and controlling the situation, such that all the way down his command, everybody realises that the situation has changed. The situation is now not about hammering the daylights out of each other. It's about actually disengaging, stabilising, and preparing for a ceasefire to come in, and therefore, we should not take -- or he would be ordering his troops not to take any offensive actions that could negate the movement towards a ceasefire, and he would probably also be giving instructions as to: Do not be provoked. My intention is that whatever happens, we must bring this ceasefire about. On our side, we are not going to provoke the enemy, but we must also make sure that we do not allow the enemy to provoke us. And therefore, he may be saying things like: Even if you are receiving incoming artillery fire, you are not to respond. Or: Even if you are receiving sniper fire, you are not to respond. In this instance, he would be saying, I suggest, something like: It is more important at this stage to keep our heads down, keep our guard up, and do our best to disengage, in order that the ceasefire can be brought about. Now, that is not easy. It's highly complex. It's a change of intent. It's a change in orders amongst soldiers who are in combat. And therefore, the onus on that commander and the whole of the chain of command is absolutely clear. This very positive command and control has now got to be exerted to bring this change of intent round. This is like moving an oil tanker. This is not going to happen by automatic. Anything can knock the ceasefire off line, and it's going to need very positive control and a very tight grip all the way down the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would there be an expectation that the commander, the higher commander, review pre-existing concerns or problems in his area of responsibility and factor those into what needs to be done to make sure the ceasefire takes place?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think one of the things the commanders at all levels would be doing would be asking themselves: What are the sort of things that could go wrong? What are the sort of actions that might happen which I should alert my troops to in order that they take the correct actions in those events? So, for example, whereas yesterday incoming artillery would be met firmly with outgoing artillery, today my instructions will be: It's more important to go firm, stay protected, and do nothing to upset events, in order that we will be complying with everything that is required to bring this ceasefire into effect. So they will be asking themselves, at all levels -- I mean, down at grass roots levels, the platoon commanders in the front-line trenches who have been receiving sniper fire and returning it, and doing their best to discover where these snipers are coming from, they will be giving their troops instructions: Right. We're heading for a ceasefire. Much more important now not to take any actions that might knock that off course. I want you all to stay heads down, sentries out, on guard, no return fire unless I authorise it. Is probably what he'd be saying, because he now realises he has to take a firm grip because the events have changed. And similar things will be happening at all levels.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would any particular attention be paid to problem units or disciplinary problems from the past that would not be appropriate to be repeated, that could derail?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, that comes down to commander's knowledge. If he is aware, if he is aware that there's a problem brigade or a problem unit or a problem company, you know, depending on what level we're talking about, and they're a problem because they have very strong soldiers and a very weak commander, and in the past they've tended to get out of control, or in the past they've taken actions without authority, that sort of thing. If he's got that sort of problem at any level in his command, he would certainly be focussing on that and taking whatever actions he deemed necessary to ensure that that problem unit did not create the conditions where he could not achieve his operational strategic intent of bringing in the ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Might that include removal of the unit or personnel therefrom?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might. I mean, it could.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I would temper that by realism. I mean, if this problem unit -- if I have not considered it to be so much of a problem that I haven't removed the commander already, well, then, what I probably need now is extra supervision and extra tight grip, because if I suddenly decide I ought to remove that guy, well, I've probably left it a bit late. I probably should have removed him before. But the answer to your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. question is yes. If he thought that was necessary, if he had that little confidence or that much concern about that commander or whatever, then he is quite entitled and empowered, and indeed he may think he has an abject requirement to remove him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm going to try to ask just a couple more questions and finish up very quickly. But if an attack on a protected site did occur during attack under these circumstances on a military objective, what emergency measures should the higher commander take or have taken to terminate the attack on the protected site?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Well, assuming it is clear that the protected site is being attacked, and one would assume that situation reports are flowing up and down the chain of command and that commanders are becoming aware, even if they're not aware right at the beginning, are becoming aware that a protective site is coming under attack in the course of another attack, I would expect the commanders immediately to start -- knowing or assuming that this is against standing orders and outside the commander's intent, I would expect commanders at all levels immediately to focus on that. The first question they would ask is: Why is that happening? Because it's not inconceivable that, you know, a rocket battery is engaging them and causing heavy casualties from the protected site, in which case, those that have sighted the rocket battery at the protected site are in the wrong, and there's a very real issue there about what you do about it, protected site or not. So the first question you would ask is: Why is that protected site being engaged? And if there is no satisfactory answer, or if the answer is such that he does not think that the threat emerging from the area of that protected site is worth the firepower being put on it, in other words, there may be in the area of the protected site some fire coming but it's not consequential. Then the commander would have an onus to comply with the orders he's been given and check firing on that protected site. And that would be the immediate commander. The commander who commands the assets that are engaging the protected site. And if he doesn't do that, his superior commander has an onus to stop it. And if he doesn't do that, his superior commander has an onus to stop it, on the assumption that the information would be travelling up the chain of command. Protected sites are sensitive. Protected sites have been the subject of specific orders from on high. On high will want to know about that. So, you know, there are checks at various levels. But that's the process that will be gone through, which one could -- which one might assume would lead to an order to check firing on the protected site, regardless of the ongoing attack on another objective.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: General, if that protected site had been the subject of a standing order which indicated that under no circumstances, under no circumstances, should there be engagement of that site, would that alter your response at all? Under no circumstances, for argument, could include even if attack were forthcoming therefrom.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, if the order is "under no circumstances," then commanders would be unwise to engage that protected site. However, if the hypothetical situation is such that there really is very serious fire coming from that protected site, and by effective it means it is causing casualties or negating his ability to achieve his objective, then he would have a duty to go back up the chain of command and say: Look, I know the orders are "under no circumstances, engage this site," but you should be aware that I'm taking considerable casualties from fire coming from that protected site, and unless I engage it, these will be the implications. I will not achieve your objective or I will have to call off the attack or I will take serious casualties. It would then be for the superior commander to decide what he's going to do about that. Does he say: These are very special circumstances, and under these circumstances, and I am prepared to justify my decision later, I would try and suppress that fire. Or does he say: No. Under no circumstances means under no circumstances. It's just too precious, that site. If the price of not engaging that site is we call off the attack, then we call off the attack. He will have to go through that thought process.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would this be consistent, General, with your previous view that disengagement, given the strategic objective, may well be called for and further -- any engagement of a protected site should not even be considered, given the overall need to carry out the strategic objective?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is consistent with my view that the commander realises that there are very serious actions he is now going to have to take to ensure that he does not create the conditions where this sort of thing could happen. So that's what will be in the commander's mind, and so he will have issued instructions in order to ensure that the hornet's nest, if I can put it like that, is not stirred up, such that he will not find himself in this position. If he does find himself in this position, given the fact that we're meant to be heading for a ceasefire, that's actually the strategic intent, we're heading for a ceasefire. Somehow we've got ourselves in a position where the hornet's nest has been stirred up. Well, actually, his orders would almost certainly be, the strategic intent is head for the ceasefire, disengage, stop, stop, stop, go back to where you started. This is not easy. But, you know, in simple terms, that's where he will be coming from. We seem -- this seems to have completely run out of control, for whatever reason. So yes, I believe under those circumstances he would be saying: You know, stop firing. Disengage. Go back to where you started.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: General, if no meaningful inquiry or appropriate disciplinary action were undertaken following an unlawful attack or action, would you draw any conclusion as to the commander's actual intent?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If no disciplinary action is taken at any level following events that are specifically forbidden, then at all levels that connive - and I use that word deliberately - that connive in turning a blind eye to the disobedience to standing orders, that would mean that up to and including all levels of connivance, those sorts of actions lie well within what is deemed acceptable and what is intent.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: General, what disciplinary action, then, having said what you just said, would you expect to be taken if the unlawful action by the subordinate units was in accordance with the commander's intent?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the unlawful action was in accordance with the commander's intent, then I would not be surprised if no action was taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: General, in this instance, does the existence of an unfavourable command climate negate the responsibility of the commander for the acts of his subordinates?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The responsibility of the commander for the acts of his subordinates at all levels is vested in him by the authority of his commander -- by his authority as the commander. So whatever command climate is being created at whatever level, that does not negate his responsibility. In fact, creating the climate where proper actions are taken is very much part of his responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General Pringle. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Somers. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. If I may borrow the stand from Ms. Somers for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Pringle. I am Goran Rodic, an attorney at law from Podgorica, from the Defence team of General Strugar. I shall be asking you questions concerning the findings that you have expounded in this particular matter. In connection with the last part of your testimony during the examination-in-chief, which I suppose we shall agree mainly dealt with hypothetical situations, can you please tell me whether everything that you have talked about in the last part of your testimony, whether you have Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. experience to illustrate this with -- from your personal experience or from the practice of others on the basis of which you provided your answers.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rodic. Yes. I think I can say that I do have personal experience, certainly in terms of dealing and thinking through those sorts of events through a series of staff colleges and war colleges, through a whole series of exercises and manoeuvres, and through active, live operations in places like Northern Ireland and Bosnia. They may not have been specifically the same as the hypothetical situation we were talking about, but I would consider that my training experience has equipped me with the knowledge to understand exactly what the implications are and what the actions required of a commander under those circumstances would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I suppose that these examples also refer to the professional army that you belonged to.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm more talking about the aspects of command that would be executed by the commanders, and in general terms, we've been talking about relatively high-level commanders, which I would assume would be commanders of some experience and probably professional themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were you trained in how other armies are being organised, conducted, outside the British army, that is?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That has been part of one's training, through staff colleges and exercises. For example, for the first, what, two-thirds of my career, we were focussed predominantly on two things. One was the IRA, republican terrorism in Ireland. But more pertinent to your question is that of course NATO was lined up against the Warsaw Pact, and therefore, all exercises, manoeuvres, all staff colleges, all war colleges, would study, in particular, Warsaw Pact armies, styles, doctrines, as part of military education.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While our memory is still fresh in connection with this particular situation that you described during the last part of your testimony, I will be asking you several questions in that particular regard. In these hypotheses and theories, to the effect that a commander has launched an attack without approval, of his own initiative, that is, please respond to this question: What if, irrespective of a ceasefire, which, for instance, has been violated over a lengthy period of time in 17 incidents, and on this 17th or 18th instance, the commander of the battalion is suffering great consequences on that account, and heavy casualties are being inflicted on his troops, how would you assist such a situation? And if that commander is engaging a military target, wishing to neutralise the enemy's artillery, the site which is inflicting these losses on him, in other words?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You paint a very uncomfortable picture for the commander in question. This commander will find himself in some dilemma. On the one hand, he is, I assume, preparing for a ceasefire; and on the other hand, he is having to deal with enemy actions that are going to make disengagement, which is what I was talking about before, quite difficult. Now, here I would say that it's very important for this commander to have a very clear idea on his higher commander's intent. What is it that is important? Is it more important to take the actions required to bring the ceasefire about, or is it more important to launch some sort of counter-attack, in the full knowledge that that will negate the ceasefire? So you paint an uncomfortable picture, but that's the sort of picture that commanders are paid to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I object for a moment, in that, as I have read the question, it appears that the discussion about taking hits, and perhaps I'm wrong, refers to past actions and that an unauthorised ceasefire results from past actions where losses, et cetera, are incurred. And I wonder if counsel could clarify that, because, as I read it, I don't see that that's the -- that the response matches the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't see the limitation that you do, I'm afraid, Ms. Somers, because while there was reference to a 17 or 18 incidents over a lengthy period, it then went on to say: "And is suffering great consequences. Heavy casualties are being inflicted." It was speaking in the question as it was posed about immediate casualties being inflicted of a heavy nature, as I read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarification. I did not see it that way, and I wasn't clear how it was intended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it's in that context that the answers were given. Is that right, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right. I mean, the picture I had in my mind was a picture painted where I, as the commander in question, am receiving considerable artillery fire and taking heavy casualties and am meant to be heading for a ceasefire, and what am I going to do about it? I tried to answer it in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps to clarify the situation for you, to amplify on it a bit: The commander -- or no. Not the commander. Larger strategic group is situated on an area covering 30.000 square kilometres, which is approximately the area for Northern Ireland. In this area, there are five garrisons. The problems are different. All kinds of problems. So I'm speaking about the situation where there is loss of life, where combat and military operations are taking place. This large strategic group consists of a number of corps. We have the commander of the strategic group, there are the corps commanders, the brigade commanders, the battalion, company commanders, and so on and so forth. The task of the strategic group is not to conquer a certain portion of territory but to block, to impose a blockade on that part of territory in order to protect from the military aspect the back of this strategic group and to preclude the influx, the supply of armaments and the arming of paramilitary formations in this part of territory which is to be blockaded. Also, the situation obtains where the strategic group in question is in any case much superior to the paramilitary units which are situated, which are deployed in the part of the blockade, the territory in question. Let me also emphasise that the strategic group does not wish to take that territory, nor to make any incursions, in-raids, into that territory. Over a protracted period, from that territory, the units and the corps which is holding this zone of responsibility and of operations, by applying the tactic of negotiations and the striking of ostensible ceasefires which are violated, which have been violated for 17 or so times, this situation which I previously explained ensues, which is the commander who suffered losses proceeds from that point to neutralise the military point which has been inflicting losses on his troops. Have I clarified my point, and can you please then give me your reaction to it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that was a statement or a question, Mr. Rodic? But I'll try and make what I can of that. What you're describing are the extensive responsibilities of an operational-level commander. I would not pretend that those responsibilities are not wide, various, and extremely demanding. And his attention will be focussed on a large number of issues for which he has a staff to assist him in controlling that. But he will also have his main effort, and his main effort can change from time to time, depending on events. His main effort might be focussed on a particular corps area which is heavily engaged with the enemy, which is needing considerable support, reinforcements, or whatever, and then that situation may clarify itself and front stabilised, and something else happens. And let's take, for example, now that he's faced with the strategic requirement to bring in a ceasefire on another part of his front. Well, now this is absolutely operational-level business, and his focus, assuming the rest of his area is not calling for his attention at higher priority, his focus will now turn, and his own personal main effort, will now turn to this particular issue and his energies will be devoted to that. So what I'm trying to say is although the operational-level commander has a wide span of command, that is, a large number of units under command, a large geographical area of operational responsibility, he also has a staff and he personally will be focussing his main effort on what he considers to be the most important thing at the time. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I painted too broad a picture. But let's move on. The situation which you explained with the battalion commander, if I told you hypothetically speaking, what if, for instance, we have a battalion commander who is mentally unstable and an excess of this sort occurs? Would this be of bearing on -- would this be of individual influence on the specific situation, regardless of the command climate, regardless of the orders, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have a battalion commander who is mentally unstable, his brigade commander has a serious and immediate problem, and he should have been removed already.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What if such an immediate first or second superior commander who is in the most frequent of contacts with this commander does not inform the superior command on time of this particular situation?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The responsibility to remove a mentally unstable battalion commander lies with the brigade commander. He doesn't need to receive authority from elsewhere. He probably has to inform higher up the chain of command, but he doesn't need to receive their authority to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And if, for instance, in connection with this incident that we talked about, the excess on the part of the battalion commander, the corps commander, within which is the brigade and the battalion that we are talking about, what if, in connection with this incident, he submits a report to the highest command within the armed forces, and then receives specific instructions from that command, for instance, to undertake an investigation, and if that commander, corps commander, does conduct an investigation in connection with that incident and fails to take any measures against the specific battalion commander in question? Will the situation regarding that incident be a closed matter then?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm just reading your question again. As I understand it, you're saying to me that if this mentally unstable battalion commander has been investigated up to -- or if the matter that he is mentally unstable has been addressed up to corps level, and at corps level, the fact that there is a mentally unstable battalion commander is deemed to be acceptable, and therefore, no action is required, is that the end of the matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Perhaps you did not understand me properly. I shall try to explain my question to enable you to reply. So I gave you a hypothetical thesis, to the effect that the battalion commander is mentally unstable. You replied to my question, saying that that commander should have been dealt with by the brigade commander. Now I'm asking you, in connection with a situation -- or rather, the incident caused by the mentally unstable battalion commander, despite the fact that there was a ceasefire on, so he provoked this incident by seeking to neutralise the enemy's fire point, which was inflicting heavy losses on him, so if the corps commander, within the composition of which is the battalion, reports on this incident to the highest army leadership of the army in question and receives from that leadership instructions to conduct an investigation into the incident, the way it happened, what were the circumstances of the incident, and the corps commander does undertake such an investigation but fails to undertake any measures against the battalion commander, can the matter be considered, the entire incident, can it be considered to be a finished matter at the level of the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand your question now. To have a commanding officer who is blatantly transgressing orders, for whatever reason, mental instability or whatever, is a matter that would come to the attention, I would suggest, to the highest levels of command in that theatre. The fact that an investigation is ordered into the conduct of that commanding officer is correct, would be correct, and depending on the results of that investigation, the corps commander, if that is the level of authority committed to deal with a commanding officer, if the corps commander decides to dismiss the charges, and that is within his powers, then that would be the end of the matter, depending on whether the corps commander's superior was content that a proper investigation had been conducted, the results of that investigation had been properly assessed, and the appropriate -- and the matter had been dealt with in the appropriate manner. So what I'm saying is if, hypothetically, the corps commander dismisses the charge as a whitewash, hypothetically speaking, then the corps commander's superior commander has an onus to take action, not only on the original transgression of the battalion commander, but on the corps commander who has connived in a whitewash, hypothetically speaking, if that's your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I shall clarify the last part of this hypothesis. The brigade commander, in any case, who is in charge of the battalion commander, has the authority to replace him. The corps commander who is in charge of the investigation in any case can always take any measures to replace or discipline such a battalion commander. During this investigation, let us say not the first superior command of the corps commander, but the highest command has been informed. I ask you now whether, in this case, the corps commander has closed the matter concerning the incident and the battalion commander. He has found him to be not responsible. After the investigation, the corps commander finds that he is not responsible for the incident.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assuming that the corps commander's superior is content with the way the investigation has been conducted and that it has been investigated rigorously and analysed properly and a reasonable judgement has been made, then that would be the end of the matter, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Rodic, or is there something you want just to tidy up?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question connected to this one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you say the superior corps commander, can you make this more specific, in relation to the hypothetical situation where the corps commander is the commander of the army, and then there is the General Staff, and finally, the highest military command in that army, the Federal Secretary. The Federal Secretary, or the Minister of Defence, issued an order to have the incident investigated, and in the General Staff, and the Federal Secretary have been informed of the results of the investigation, were you referring to them, that if they're satisfied there has been a rigorous examination and that the battalion commander has been exonerated, then that is then the end of the matter?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was trying to answer your question in the context of the rather lengthy question I previously had, which I've had a certain amount of difficulty with, where there is an operational group in this chain of command which has under command a number of corps, brigades, and independent units. And what I was saying is that if the corps commander has effectively dismissed the charge in question, then -- and let's be more specific here, then. If the corps commander's superior, that is, the -- in this instance, the operational group commander, is content with the way the investigation has been conducted, then the matter would end with the corps commander, information would go up to the operational group and on up to the federal level, Ministry of Defence, and that's the end of the matter. But there are quite a lot of assumptions in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify a bit. While the incident is still under way, it's still going on, the Minister of Defence is informed about it. The incident is still happening, and the corps commander has come to report to the Minister of Defence in connection with the situation. It is then that he is given instructions to conduct an investigation. After the investigation, he reports directly to the Minister of Defence, who is at the head of the army, about the results of the investigation. Is the matter then closed? Is that the end of the matter?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would assume -- well, you seem to have skipped out -- we've skipped out the level between corps commander and Federal Ministry of Defence. You're painting a situation where the corps commander is dealing directly with the Federal Ministry of Defence bypassing the corps commander's superior officer. Under those circumstances, I would expect the corps commander's superior officer, the operational group commander, to take an interest in what is going on, (a), inquire from the federal Ministry of Defence why are they dealing with this issue over his head; and (b), to demand of the corps commander the same question. So, from the operational group commander's perspective, unless he's absolutely content to just let it run and be bypassed, I would say that's not the end of the issue, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's a convenient moment now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the 20-minute morning break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pringle, answering my questions before the break, I mentioned a strategic group and the army. I used only those terms. In your response, you mentioned an operative group. Can you tell me how you came by this?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Operational group. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because in general terms, I have read a number of documents relating to the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what you read?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read a large number of documents about JNA doctrine, one of which I was quoting yesterday. I have read outlined descriptions of the events that are under discussion in this Court. So I'm generally aware of the issues and the command chain, if I can put it like that, relating to this case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me which documents in connection with JNA doctrine have you read?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I've been involved as a military consultant to the ICTY, assisting the military analysis team and the lawyers on a number of cases. This is the first case where I've actually appeared as a witness in Court. In the course of all that, over the last, oh, 18 months, I suppose, I have read quite a lot of JNA doctrine documents, including, for example, this one I quoted yesterday, the application of international law of war. I've read the two references in my statement that I have written. That's the command and control one and the other one, reference B was this international law. I've also read the corps doctrine and SOPs and quite a lot of other documents whose titles I can't give you at the moment, but no doubt I could look them up if you really wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In which team did you -- which team did you work for as a consultant?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- my primary point of contact was the military analysis team.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is this a Prosecution team?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I'm aware, no. That is a group of predominantly ex-military who support military analysis in support of these cases. Whether that is part of the Prosecution team, you'll have to ask somebody else, I'm afraid, but that's what it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This ex-military team, analysing cases, the cases before this Tribunal, who do you send the results of your analysis to?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the military analysis team has just changed, and -- very recently, and I was sort of tasked by and reporting to Peter Nicholson, the head of the military analysis team.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Does he work for the Prosecution of this Tribunal, the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he's now moved to work for the International Criminal Court. Previously, as the head of the military analysis team, he -- I'm afraid I'm not -- I don't know whether formally he worked for the Office of the Prosecutor or whether they are independent and advising as necessary. You'll have for ask, I'm afraid, an expert on the organisation of the ICTY to get the proper answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any documents from him indicating his position, who he worked for?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've received a large number of documents from him, and I've read a large number of documents on my various visitations to The Hague. The military analysis team provides military analysis to the lawyers here in ICTY, so that they - because so many of these cases are based on military issues - so that they understand what the issues are.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Does he work for the Office of the Prosecutor, or did he submit these results to Defence counsel acting for the accused before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly the analysis and assistance is provided to the lawyers who form part of the Prosecution, but I think that any evidence or statements that are to be used in Court - correct me if I'm wrong - but I think they are also supplied to the Defence counsel as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you participate in making analyses in connection with the Dubrovnik operation?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you tell me why you did not put this into your CV?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The detail in a CV. does not have to extend anything other than what areas of expertise or where a person has worked. It is irrelevant to putting it in a CV

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That appears to be the position, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You said you received a summary of the events that are being examined in this case. Can you tell me what kind of document this was and who you received it from?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a military analysis team outline of the events and analysis of them on a number of cases, but you're talking about this particular case, which I have read and have expressed opinions on, particularly in terms of what I thought was reasonable and what I thought was unreasonable, in order, I assume, to assist in the proper construction of a case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This involves you, then, directly in the work of the office of the Prosecution, if you worked on the proper construction of this case. Why was this document not appended to your report?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. That is a conclusion that has no substance or support. It is clear that this witness is brought as a Prosecution witness. It is clear that the consultations that go into preparing any witness who is brought as the Prosecution's witness will necessarily involve interaction, and I think that the question has no purpose other than to confuse on a responsibility that does not lie with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: To some degree, I'm in sympathy with what you say, Ms. Somers, but there remains unclear, because the Chamber has no knowledge, the precise role of the group or team of which the witness is a member and Mr. Rodic has been asking questions. At the moment, the witness is unable to help him on the answer that he really wants, that is, is this part of the Prosecution or otherwise? Now, you and I know that this is quite separate from the question of the evidence given by the witness here in this Court, but for reasons that are understandable, the Defence would like to know the answer to that question. Are you able to help?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I just comment, though? Your Honour has just made a -- in his discussion with me, a member of the Prosecution team, and the witness has not indicated that he was a member of the Prosecution team, but rather, that he was working with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What have I said about Prosecution team?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I believe it says -- the witness is -- the precise role of the group or team of which the witness is a member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's not a Prosecution team; it's the Defence analysis group or team, or whatever the precise name was. I have not had an answer, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I understood it to mean that there was -- that he was part of a Prosecution team and the link -- the MAT's role, he indicated, or its relationship, was not -- perhaps -- Your Honour, perhaps if I've misunderstood you, then I apologise. I thought it was the suggestion of the Prosecution. I may have confused your question. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But I was asking whether you can assist us with the answer to the question that Mr. Rodic is pursuing and which the witness cannot assist us with.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And the question specifically is: Is the MAT part of the Prosecution? The MAT is under the Office of the Prosecution. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And that he is not a member of it, I can also indicate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Who is not a member of it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, does that help, Mr. Rodic? I've tried to cut through a number of things there to get you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It does assist. And my question was in connection with something this witness stated, and that is that he conducted broader military analysis in a military team, broader military analysis of this case, which were submitted to the Prosecutor. So it is obvious for which side he was working and what he was doing. That is why we have already intervened, because it was evident during the examination-in-chief. Why, then, was the Prosecutor putting her questions in hypothetical terms, when it was evident that, although the questions were hypothetical, the witness was not talking off the top of his head?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have attempted already, Mr. Rodic, to explain the basis upon which the Chamber perceives this evidence. The witness has not presumed to discuss the particular facts of this case. He was not a party involved in them. He had no personal knowledge. He has come along to speak only as a person familiar with matters military, to speak from that experience, to say, as a matter of military practice and theory, the questions you pose to me hypothetically suggest answer A or answer B. Now, that is the limit to which the evidence of this witness has gone, and he does not presume to tell us anything about what happened in this particular case. From what little I know, I would think he knows nothing of what happened in this particular case of his own knowledge. So very rightly, he has not sought to suggest what may have happened from his reading or what he may have learnt from other people. We, as a Chamber, will rely upon what people can tell us in evidence who have actual knowledge of what did happen, and they may or may not include your client in due course. We don't learn from what other people hear about it and then try to theorise about the actual events. But we may be assisted by learning what is the general military understanding or expectation in a certain hypothetical situation, and it's in that area that this witness has given his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes. I take note of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In connection with your last reply concerning the hypothetical incident and the battalion commander, I now put the following question to you: If the commander, let us say of the operational group, since you dealt with this, knows about a direct instruction from the Ministry of Defence given to a corps commander, and is informed that, after conducting an investigation, the corps commander has informed the Minister of Defence of the results of the investigation, would you expect the operational group commander to interfere and get involved and to examine the final results, the final conclusions reached by the General Staff and the Minister of Defence?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I would expect the operational group commander to wonder why the Ministry of Defence is dealing direct to a corps commander subordinate to the operational group commander. This may be standard operational procedure in the JNA. I don't know. But in my experience, I would find that rather irregular, and therefore, I would expect the operational group commander, at the least, to ask questions as to why it is happening like that. And assuming that the operational group commander, as the higher-level commander has complete authority for - responsibility - has complete responsibility for everything that happens in his area, I would find the fact that he was being cut out and his opinion was not being asked somewhat strange.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What you are now saying seems as if you were speaking of your own personal impressions. I'm asking you specifically: Would the commander of an operational group be authorised to review a decision concerning an incident which was done between the Minister of Defence and the corps commander who submitted the report? Are you saying that the operational group commander should review the final decision issued by the Minister of Defence?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would expect the operational group commander who is in the chain of command between the corps commander and the Minister of Defence, to be involved in satisfying himself that the investigation in hand has been properly conducted because ultimately he is responsible. I mean, I could go on and pose some hypothetical considerations to you, but I say again: I would expect the operational group commander at least to inquire from the Ministry of Defence why they're dealing with one of his subordinate corps, bypassing him. I find that irregular.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Assuming that the commander of the operational group was bypassed for a reason, would he then be authorised to review the final decision?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think you'd find the answer to that in the JNA's disciplinary doctrine, which will lay down the role of those in the chain of command in reviewing such incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In answer to my last question, would you please tell us specifically yes or no. That is, reviewing a final decision issued by the Minister of Defence, by the commander of an operational group in the situation that has been described in detail, what would your answer be? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the investigation has been carried out in accordance with the military law in place in the JNA and the regulations that back that up, if that has been done, then the answer is yes. I cannot tell you whether that was the case or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: We are now speaking in hypothetical terms. Would the superior command of the operative group commander carry this out?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Carry what out?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Reviewing the final decision of the Minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The final decision of the Minister of Defence, I assume, would be common to all ministries of defence, and that would be final. What I have been saying is whether the proper steps that are laid down, that should be taken before it reaches the Ministry of Defence have all been taken. If they have all been taken, then that's fine. If they haven't all been taken, then the Ministry of Defence, I would suggest, is taking whatever decisions it's taking based on irregular practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The hypothesis that you're including in your reservation, I will tell you the following: If the hypothetical corps commander has carried out an investigation in accordance with directions from the Minister of Defence and in accordance with military regulations, which he's certainly familiar with, reported directly to the Minister of Defence about this and then a final decision has been issued on the situation, does then the commander of an operational group have the ability to interfere and to review the decision made by the Minister of Defence? The question is quite clear, and it can be answered with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is clear, but I don't think it can be answered with a yes or a no, because in the hypothesis you're suggesting, the highest-level operational commander has been bypassed, and yet that highest-level operational commander has specific responsibilities, including, in law, to ensure that everything that happens in his command is happening within the law. So he should be, in my opinion, satisfied, and therefore involved, that the investigation you are talking about has been conducted properly and proper conclusions have been come to. On that basis, it would go to the Ministry of Defence, and the Ministry of Defence ratifies it or not, as the case may be, but the operational group commander is entirely satisfied that he has taken the proper actions. Now, I cannot answer your question with a straight yes or no, because that critical link in the chain you are leaving out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The critical link that you keep insisting upon is something I have described hypothetically as follows: The commander of the operational group knows about the incident. The commander of the operational group knows about the direct instructions given by the Minister of Defence to the corps commander. He is informed of the final decision made by the Minister of Defence. And in this hypothetical situation, the Minister of Defence has bypassed the commander of the operational group, but why he has done this is the Minister of Defence's business. He has reasons of his own. But this situation is very specific, concrete. And when I ask you whether, after the Minister of Defence has issued a final decision, you would expect the commander of the operational group to review his decision; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hypothetical picture you have painted has now brought in the added dimension that the operational group commander is fully aware of what is going on, and the assumption is there that the operational group commander is in agreement with the way that the affair is being conducted. In other words, he has stepped to one side and, if you like, abrogated his authority willingly, in which case he has, for whatever reason, ceased to take an interest in the affair, and if he is content to do that and the corps commander's decision is ratified by the Minister of Defence in stepping aside willingly, that operational group commander agrees that that is the end of the affair. So under those circumstances, I can give you a yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I must admit that I admire your persistence to adapt my hypothetical situation to your hypothetical situation instead of responding to the hypothetical situation that I'm painting for you, without any additions. But I believe this was sufficiently clear so that I will move on. In the period from 1998 to 2001, you were chief of General Staff of the joint staff of the army of Great Britain, were you not? I'm sorry. A member of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was about to say in response to your question: If only that had been the case. Sadly, it was not. No. Between 1998 and 2001, I was the chief of staff and director of operations of the permanent joint headquarters, which is the joint staff of the armed forces, not just the army; the armed forces of Great Britain.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In your CV, I could read that you had a great deal of cooperation conducted with civilian agencies and the NGOs, non-governmental sector, that you had close cooperation with them. Does this refer only to Great Britain? Is it only confined to Great Britain, or to other places where you served?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've had close contact with civilian agencies and NGOs, predominantly in the Balkans, but in planning purposes, from the permanent joint headquarters, that was an aspect of planning that we had to deal with and be aware of, because in the sort of operations we were conducting, civilian agencies and NGOs would be playing a key role.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me: In this extensive CV, why is it not included that you cooperated with the military analyst team of the OTP of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We've had that question, and we've dealt with it, haven't we, Mr. Rodic? That came up very early.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I'll go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the period from 1992 to 1994, you were deputy head of assessment staff, and as far as I can see, you reported to the joint intelligence committee of the cabinet office and prepared analytical assessments of the situation, inter alia, also in the Balkans; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Or not in the Balkans; concerning the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you gathered information from open and secret sources?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the role of the assessment staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you reported, assessed, and analysed the rapidly deteriorating situation concerning the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In addition to this reporting, did you have any other role in connection with the deteriorating situation in the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such -- I'm not sure what you have in mind. I mean, my responsibility, as one of the deputy heads of the assessment staff, was to provide intelligence analysis from open and secret sources to the joint intelligence committee on a number of areas of responsibility, and in my case, one of which was the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Specifically referring to the Balkans, these analyses have to do with the former SFRY?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those analyses had involved analysis on the complete situation in the Balkans during the time period specified, which would have included the SFRY, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: At the time, were you involved in any way in any operations concerning the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were these analyses of yours, and intelligence reports, were they used against anyone at the time the situation in the SFRY deteriorated in that period?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the purpose of the reports. The reports were produced to inform the highest levels of government about the assessment of the situation. They were designed to inform ministers in the various departments of state as to what the UK's assessment of the situation was. They were not designed to be used against anyone or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you engage in strategic and operational planning of extensive, expensive, and potentially very risky operations, less and more complex, and were you in charge of a team that was in charge of organising the participation of the army and organising the campaign and the possible operation in Montenegro with the participation of the three arms of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
