utterances.text: Now you have moved out of my time in the cabinet office to my time as chief of staff, director of operations in the permanent joint headquarters, where, yes, I did involve -- I was involved in strategic and operational planning in a wide variety of operations round the world, which I touched on yesterday, including the Balkans. And, sorry, you've asked me specifically about Montenegro. Yes, and contingency planning that might have involved Montenegro or actions that might need to be taken in the event of various events coming about.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Where was this plan compiled? Where was it prepared, and for what particular purpose?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The permanent joint headquarters was responsible for contingency planning for a whole host of operations round the world. We were obviously thinking about potential operations in the Balkans up until such time, really, that NATO arrived in Kosovo, by which time I was beginning to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What I'm specifically interested in is this part. So being in charge of a team that had to plan and organise the campaign of possible operations in Montenegro and Kosovo, with the participation, with the contribution of the three arms of the armed forces. For what period was this? Sorry. Was it in the 1980, 1990, 1999, the 1999 campaign that you drew up these plans for? That is what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was involved in the Balkans for so long, over so many years, that these campaigns rather sort of merge into one. But we're talking about the period -- we're talking about the period after Bosnia and before NATO moved into Kosovo. Now, that was -- you can remind me. That was when? 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Possibly, although I was not on that team, but I can assume. Can you tell us what kind of an operation and campaign these were supposed to be and what was the objective of it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think I can tell you that. All I can tell you is that it was normal contingency planning that any nation would conduct under those conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you refer to a campaign, I assume that the forces of the British army, as part of the NATO forces, should probably have come to the area of Montenegro and Kosovo, with the three branches, the three arms of the armed forces participating, as you state here. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the British forces were a contributory part of the NATO forces that did enter Kosovo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was an assessment made of the campaign for Montenegro as well? Was the situation foreseen whereby the forces would also have to enter Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Plainly, we were thinking about that, as we were thinking about all options, depending on how events were going to evolve. But plainly, our responsibilities included thinking about every operation, every conceivable operation, that might be needed. That's a normal part of contingency planning. If I told you that at the same time we were also doing contingency planning on Sierra Leone, you would get the flavour of the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I intrude, Mr. Rodic? Are we talking about 1999 still in your questioning?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I suppose that this period is in question, associated with this particular campaign in Montenegro that I'm asking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm trying to discern the relevance of that to the issues in this case, which are eight years earlier. Can you help me there?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance has to do with the actual capacity in which this witness is participating in this particular case. But if you say so, I can move on to another area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I think we've got a clear picture of the various capacities in which the witness has acted over the years, so I'd encourage you to move on at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether you were familiar with the situation in the former SFRY in 1990, 1991, and 1992? Were you well acquainted with the situation in connection with the duties that you were performing?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my time in the cabinet office, as I said, one of the -- my responsibilities was to provide the assessments on the Balkan area, and therefore, during that period, I was -- I became pretty well acquainted with the situation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me briefly: Have you ever heard of any state in the world having three armies?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any single state having three armies? No. Unless you're talking about Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That is what I had in mind. Tell me: Have you read the indictment in this case?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm pausing because I'm -- I don't think I have. I don't think I have. Indeed, I only asked yesterday somebody: What is the charge in this case? But I might have done. I don't think I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: As you say that you may have read it, I will take this opportunity to remind you of Count 4 of this indictment, and if you can -- if you do recall it, please tell me. As an officer in commanding duty in the JNA, Pavle Strugar was duty-bound to abide by regulations, so Pavle Strugar was obliged to respect the JNA regulations contained in the 1983 strategy of armed struggle, the law on total National Defence from 1992, the law on service in the armed forces from 1985, the rules of service from 1985, and the regulations on the application of the international law of war in the armed forces of the SFRY from 1998. Are you familiar with this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me: Do I recall reading that? I don't. But none of that surprises me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you, before coming to this Court to testify, did you study these regulations which I have just enumerated?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some of those we have been talking about already. I said I had read, over a fairly considerable amount of time, in the course of my duties as a consultant to the military analysis team, quite a lot of JNA documentation; indeed, one of those documents you're quoting there is the one I was holding up yesterday. So a number of those documents I will have -- I will have read, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were the documents that you just quoted the only reference material that you used to get acquainted with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have been party to military analysis team reports as well, on which I have commented in the past. So my becoming acquainted with the JNA is not confined simply to reading JNA documentation, although that is a critical part. And in reading JNA doctrine, I have to say, I was extremely struck by how good and thorough it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I must interrupt you. This was not my question. In your report, you spoke about the reference material which you drew upon when you were preparing your opinion, your finding. I'm asking you whether this was the only material that you had read in connection with the armed forces of the SFRY prior to stating your opinion and rendering your testimony.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I've answered that question in the negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you not feel that that is insufficient for drawing up a complete report about the armed forces and the regulations of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't drawn up a complete report about the armed forces and the regulations of the armed forces. What I have done is -- and the only bit of written documentation I was asked to provide was to answer some questions specifically related to command, which we went through yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you feel that the documents you listed in your expert report are sufficient for you to speak with precision on command and leadership in the armed forces of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document I wrote, although it draws on two documents in particular concerning the doctrine of the SFRY, was written very much in the abstract. And if you refer to the document, in the document is both the question I was posed in italics by the military analyst team and the answer I gave. So I wasn't trying to present a comprehensive view on the working of the JNA; I was focussed much more tightly on command and what a commander might reasonably be expected to do in certain circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the armed forces of the SFRY were, what were they made up of?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not pretend to be, nor do I hold myself up to be, an expert on the armed forces of the SFRY. But in general terms, they had an army, navy, and an air force, and then they had an extensive territorial or militia organisation as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I am inclined to disagree with you, because the regulations I asked you about, which you have not read, regulate this and say that the armed forces are a single entity consisting of the JNA and the Territorial Defence. Who commands and controls the armed forces? The SFRY, I mean.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're grilling me on my detailed knowledge of the JNA, so don't be surprised if I get your questions wrong. But I think it's the SNO.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, this is not correct. The federal -- one of the federal organs was in charge, but I will not tell you now which one. Can you tell me who established the system of command and control of the armed forces, the plans of development, the plans for the use of the armed forces, and who ensured the unity of their action.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This witness has already said he's not holding himself out to be any type of expert on the JNA or its structures, and I think that the answer -- the question has been asked and answered in a broader form earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think it would hurt, Ms. Somers, despite what you accurately put, to know whether the witness is able to answer that question. If he's not, he's not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question: Can you tell me who established the system of command and control of the armed forces, the plans for development, the plans for the use of the armed forces and who ensured the unity of their action? Who established that system? No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who, pursuant to the basic plans, enacted regulations on the plans for the use of the armed forces and the plans for their development?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, these strike me as very high-level Ministry of Defence-type questions, and as I've said, I'm not holding myself up to be an expert on that level of knowledge on the JNA in any shape or form. What I have answered questions on is what, from my experience, a reasonable commander might be expected to do under certain circumstances, which is a different area of questioning. So please continue this line of questioning, but I'm sure I won't be -- I won't be terribly good at the answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I appreciate your sincerity. I will continue my line of questioning, and I will ask you to respond as briefly as possible. Do you know who the highest command and control organ is in the armed forces of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's the head of the JNA, who sits alongside the, in English terms, Minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I have to go back to my first question. As you keep mentioning the JNA, do you draw a distinction between the armed forces of the SFRY and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think the JNA, as you said earlier, encompasses maritime, land, and air components, or army, navy, and air force, in that with a joint staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I will assist you. The armed forces of the SFRY are a unified whole. They consist of the JNA and the Territorial Defence. What you mentioned, that is, the navy, the land army, and the air force, this is what the JNA consists of in organisational terms. Do you know what the General Staff is in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The General Staff is that organ of the staff at the highest level that conducts business involving the three components that comprise the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In your view, it has the main role?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The main role of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In command.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you: Did you ever hear that the presidency of the SFRY was the highest command and control organ of the armed forces? Do you know this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this, I think, is what I referred to earlier as the SNO. But this rather reflects the military being subservient to the political.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The SNO that you mentioned stands for -- well, it's SSNO. It means the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, and it is equivalent to the Ministry of Defence. Do you know what the JNA consisted of as a component part of the armed forces of the JNA, the components that comprise any modern army in the world?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I'm aware that there was a land element, an army, a naval or maritime element, and an air element, a marine element, and you've already mentioned previously the Territorial Defence. Those are the, I believe, the component parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I have to correct you once again. As I said, these are the organisational arms of the JNA. The JNA as a component of the armed forces consisted of the commands of the units and institutions. Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we not saying the same thing? The JNA, as a component of the armed forces, consisted of the commands of the units -- are you telling me that the JNA is comprised solely of headquarters? Is that what you're suggesting? Or are you suggesting that it includes the units from the components that I've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The navy, the land army, and the air force that you mentioned as components of the armed forces of the SFRY, comprise the organisational aspect of the JNA. What you mentioned just now, I have to tell you that these three components have their own commands and units as basic elements of the organisation and composition of the JNA. But let us move on.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we're saying the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I think that the regulations from the former SFRY regulate things differently. I'm not a military expert, which is why I rely on the regulations of the former SFRY and ask you whether you had read them. Tell me, what do the combat arms consist of?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The combat arms of the army? If that's the question. Infantry, armour, engineers, gunners.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Of the JNA. We are referring now to the army, the navy, the air force, the territorial army. What do they consist of?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- I mean, if I'm understanding your question rightly, the combat arms of the army, in terms that I would understand, are those elements that I've just mentioned. The combat arms of the navy and the air force and the territorial army, I assume, unless you're asking me about the command -- detailed knowledge of the command structure, which I don't have, in the air force consists of combat, air, and supporting air; and in the navy, it consists of the maritime fleet. But I'm not exactly sure what the point behind your question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The reply to my question, according to the regulations, would be that the navy, land army, and air force consist of services and combat arms. You are now guessing based on your military experience from the British army. Can you tell me how the armed forces of the SFRY are brought up to manpower levels?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, I explained to you when we started this that I'm not an expert on the detail of the JNA or on every aspect of their regulations, and so my questions -- my answers will probably not satisfy you. But as far as I'm aware, the SFRY brought up its manpower levels through a combination of conscription, mobilisation, and - what's the right word? - mobilising, I suppose, or bringing into full-time service the territorial forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Does this correspond to enlisting -- or rather, activating reservists?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would assume that that is part of enhancing your manpower in the move to war.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell me whether volunteers can add to the manpower of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that volunteers did add to the manpower of the SFRY. Whether that was regulated or not, I'm not sure. But by volunteers -- if by "volunteers," you're referring to sort of organisations like what came to be known as Arkan's Tigers and that sort of thing, it's common knowledge that they did add to the manpower. But whether that was regulated or not, I don't know. But if your question is: Can somebody volunteer to join the armed forces? I assume the answer to that is a categoric yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. I asked you about volunteers. I did not include Arkan in that. He is something else. But from the moment that volunteers are accepted by the commands of the units they join, they are an integral component of the armed forces, and they are subordinated to the unified command of the armed forces. This is also mentioned in the numerous regulations I have mentioned, which apparently you have not come across before?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, could I just interrupt you? I've let you pursue this line of questioning at considerable length because I felt you wanted to make very clear to the Chamber what the witness said at the beginning, that is, that he had not a detailed knowledge of the legal and organisational structure of the SFRY and/or the JNA. But I think not only has the witness said that directly, but you have made it abundantly clear by now, and I would have suggested that you don't need to keep labouring the same point. We've got the message.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I got carried away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I wonder whether, having broken into your train of thought, this might be the convenient time, then, to have a further break. And that might enable you, then, to focus more directly on where you want to go in the final session. Did I see you stand, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I do have a question, Your Honour, if I might inquire. General Pringle will be leaving today, presumably, and I wondered if we might have an indication of how close we are to the conclusion of cross-examination, as I would hope, have a very brief redirect and finish today, if the Chamber is minded to allow that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How is your timetable looking, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, quite certainly I have material for cross-examination, and I'm afraid that I'm rather short of time, so that I will have to shorten my cross-examination in order to meet the deadline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good, I'm glad of that. Perhaps it's a good thing I did interrupt you when I did just a moment ago, because that helped us move on a little more quickly. Well, we'll break for just 20 minutes and then get on with it, to give you as much time as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pringle, in your report which you submitted to us, you consulted reference materials which were in use in the JNA, primarily the military academy command and control textbook. As you indicated in your report, it was signed by the head of the then-4th Department of the General Staff of the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the 4th Department of the General Staff was in charge of?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not entirely, but I imagine it was in charge of doctrine and publications in -- to deal with doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you say "doctrine," can you clarify for us what is it that you understand under the term "doctrine"?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Doctrine literally means that which is taught. I would describe the sorts of publications that you have been talking about as doctrinal publications, that is to say, publications that lay down the procedures and actions of the armed forces and the sort of operations they will conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I would not agree. This department was in charge of the basic training and regulations for the training of soldiers. Do you know that this department was not in charge of training command staff, nor was it in charge of issuing any doctrines, command doctrines?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said earlier that doctrine is literally that which is taught, so that makes perfect sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Not fully. That is why I shall ask you whether you know that the doctrine of command, according to which staff were trained to work in peacetime and wartime, was the duty of the 1st and the 2nd operations departments of the General Staff of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd have to object. This is becoming an argumentative exercise, and I don't know if this is responding to any of the matters raised on direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your objection in the first part is to style, and I agree, but I think, in the interests of speed, it's the quickest way to proceed. I think you could move fairly quickly, Mr. Rodic. You don't need to emphasise that the witness doesn't know these things. If you need to get from him which department is responsible for which, you could put that fairly directly, I'd suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know that for seven years after the reference material that you referred to in your report, after that, instructions were issued for the work of staffs in peacetime and wartime, and that was a textbook for the training of command staffs?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not part of my remit. All I was doing was referring to official JNA documentation that was relevant to the aspects of command that I'd been asked to comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: As I said, seven years after the reference material which you quote in your report, instructions were issued for the work of staffs in peacetime and wartime, and that was the textbook which was used for the training of command staffs. Are you aware of this? Yes or no, please, briefly.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I'm sure it drew on the substance of these earlier documentations, because the -- for example, the application of international laws of war in the armed forces, the SFRY, is as applicable in year one as it is in year seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes. We can concur in that view. But the application of the international law of war is not fully what this instruction represented and what it's regulated. But let's move on. When you speak about the command climate in the first part of your report, can you just briefly tell me: Who is it that creates the command climate, graphically speaking? Is it the platoon or the military top brass? Who creates the overall climate, the command climate?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In answering that, I'll repeat what I said yesterday, and that is: Every commander exudes a command climate of his own, but the most senior commander will set the tone in which all commanders operate. So the overall command climate and tone would be set by the most senior commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That's just it exactly. Tell me: What is the command climate like when half of the members of the superior command have deserted?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not a question about command climate. That's a question about disciplinary problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you what kind of an influence on the command climate does this fact have?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, assuming the most senior commander is still there, if half his superior -- if half his staff, I suppose you're saying, has deserted, he has a problem. But it's not an issue of command climate. It might be as a result of the command climate that he set. Maybe everybody is so dissatisfied with the way he is conducting his command and the manner in which he's carrying it out that that has caused them to desert. I don't know. I'm speaking hypothetically. But I'm trying to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'll try to clarify this for you. This refers to the SFRY. And then I'll ask you this: When the superior commanders of the JNA, for instance, the anti-aircraft defence and the air force commanders, desert and become the chief of the General Staff of the other side, is this or is this not a fact which affects the command climate in the JNA and the General Staff of the JNA? But briefly, please, because I will have a number of questions along the same lines.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it affects the command climate of the high-level operational commander that we're talking about in this instance, because that is one of the factors that he will take into account, and it will affect the manner in which he conducts himself and the way in which he conducts his command. It might be a challenge to him, and it may affect how he conducts himself, but it won't in itself affect the command climate; indeed, it is his responsibility to ensure that it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What is the command climate like when the individual members of the supreme command oppose the disarming of paramilitary units in a state?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I really understand your question, but the individual members of the supreme command oppose the disarming of paramilitary units in a state. Then that would create an air of uncertainty, I would have thought, lower down the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are you -- do you know what kind of a command climate we have in a brigade whose commander deserts? And I'm speaking specifically about a JNA brigade.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: A brigade whose brigade commander has deserted would find itself in a difficult position. Someone would have to assume command. I assume that would be the deputy commander of the brigade - and create his own command climate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And what is the command climate like in this brigade when the commander who took them out of the barracks and has deserted, and then knowing the positions and the locations of the soldiers of his own brigade, shelled his former soldiers and, on the first day of hostilities killed thus eight soldiers participating on the side of and commanding, of course, the units of the enemy? Does this favourably or unfavourably affect the overall command climate in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under those circumstances, I would assume that the new command climate in the brigade that has been deserted by its brigade commander, who is now shelling them, would be relatively easy to create by its new commander. They've got a -- they've got something to get their teeth stuck into and they've got a cause around which to -- around which he can build cohesion. So I don't accept that the fact that the brigade commander has deserted and is now on the other side and is now shelling them affects the -- necessarily the new command climate of the brigade which is now under a new commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know of any specific example of this kind, any specific instance?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no experience of brigade commanders deserting their brigade, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware of the fact that the operational group is a provisional organisation which had never existed before in this form and structure? I'm referring specifically to the 2nd JNA Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that that is probably the case, in the same way that ad hoc groupings were being put together to meet circumstances, to meet very difficult circumstances at the time, yes. I mean, if I can amplify that. By definition, an operational group is a grouping of formations that have been brought together for some purpose, or an operational group is a headquarters that has been provided to produce a cohesion in a command structure over a number of formations. Either way, it is not necessarily an extant and living part of the command chain, but it is a part of the command chain that has been put together to meet circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If the operational group changes its commanders over a short period of time, or rather, if its commanders have changed over a short period of time, twice, after the killing of one of the corps commanders within this operational group, objectively speaking, is the new commander encountering difficulties in his work and in his creation of a command climate, of course, difficulties associated with this situation?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander is encountering exactly what he would expect to command in war. Commanders get killed at all levels; soldiers get killed at all levels. These are part of the challenges of command. If one of his corps commanders has been killed, that's very sad, but a new corps commander would be appointed, and it would be the new corps commander's responsibility to ensure that the corps functioned properly. If the operational group commanders have changed, it is for each operational group commander, as he is appointed, to take up the mantle and the reins and create an effective command, and this is what armies are all about, particularly in war.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know how much time generally is required for a changeover of duty between two commanders at such a high level as commanders of an operational group are, which, in case you're not aware of this fact, was at the rank of an army?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this will depend on the practice of the army in question, but let us not forget that every commander is supported by a staff, and quite an extensive staff at that level. In some armies, the commanders would change over without any time at all; indeed, the system to be battle-worthy must allow for that to be able to happen because one of the commanders might get killed. I can tell you in armies that I have personal experience of, these operational group commanders would probably make a point of not meeting at all. One would leave before the other arrived. The king is dead. Long live the king. And it is the function of the staff to ensure continuity. But I don't know whether that was the practice in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is sufficient for me. Is the changeover of duty unfavourably accepted and the creation of command climate, is it unfavourably affected? Or, in other words, is the work of the commander and the creation of a climate, of a command climate, made more difficult by the fact that the commander of the operational group did not know any of the commanders of units subordinated to him within the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a challenge to the new commander, but it is not a challenge that would be unexpected at that level. And as I said yesterday, a commander, from the moment he first walks in through the door on appointment, begins to create his command climate, and under these conditions, a new commander would doubtless very quickly make it his business to get to know his subordinate commanders as quickly as possible and enable them to get to know him, in order that he can start to create the command climate which he would like to operate within his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how much time is required for the creation of a favourable command climate, given the difficulties which I referred to in the previous question?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the more time you have, the more time everybody has in the chain of command to get to know each other. But a commander can very quickly stamp his authority on his command simply by issuing an order which effectively says: I have arrived. I expect my command to carry out their duties in exactly the same way as they've been taught and in accordance with doctrine and in accordance with the rule of law, and I will be coming around to amplify that forthwith. Now, that takes five minutes. To actually get round and see all his commanders and make sure that they understand that and the importance that he stresses on that sort of thing will take longer. But he can start to impress his command climate down through the chain of command very quickly, and in particular, by using his staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You are asserting now that the command climate amounts to the issuance of communiques: I have arrived. The rules are as follows. And so on and so forth. Or is the creation of a command climate a process, as you explained in your report, which consists of a number of factors?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's both. But it's got to start somewhere. The issue you were posing me was: How does the commander start creating his command climate? But both of those aspects come into it. It then grows on the personality of the commander and the way he reacts and deals with issues, and as we were saying yesterday, the actions he takes in the course of various events, in particular, for example, events that go against the orders he's given. Now, that -- now we're talking about a climate being built on and reinforced over time as a result of actions taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If the commander who is taking over, the new commander assuming command over the operational group, did not know the units which made up the operational group, nor the zone of responsibility of that group, nor most of the commanding officers within the chain of command, and they only started to get acquainted with the operational situation upon assumption of that duty, are these aggravating factors for a new commander in the process which he needs to initiate in order to create a favourable command climate?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is plainly a challenge to a commander, but it is a similar sort of challenge that affects every commander on taking over command at almost any level. A commander may know some of his subordinates; he may not know any of them. He may be completely conversant with the operational requirements; he may need extensive briefing. That is not unusual. That is what commanders are trained to deal with. That is what their staff are trained to deal with. That's what he's paid for.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is there a difference, in view of these factors which I listed for you, is there a difference between the creation of a command climate in a company and an operational group of the rank of an army, in view of the territory, the disposition of units, the strength of the individual units? Are there differences in terms of the time required as an objective factor?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Plainly, the higher you are, the more complex it is. At the lowest level in a company, a new company commander can impress his personality on his company almost instantaneously. I mean, he can actually call all 120 of them or so around him in a small group, give them a five-minute talk, and he's pretty well made his mark, and he then builds on that. Obviously for an operational group commander it's not that simple. He has much wider responsibilities and a much wider geographical area and he's not dealing directly either; he's dealing through his subordinate commanders, which is also a different issue. But that would not be unknown to him, and he would know how to deal with that, and I suspect very quickly he would call in to him, or go to them, depending on what he thought was more appropriate and quicker, his immediate subordinate commanders to at least begin to impress his personality directly on them and to make sure that they understood what he thought was important so that they could ensure that that was impressed on their subordinate commanders, and so it goes down the chain. And then he would build on that. But there is no doubt that the higher level you are at, the more difficult -- the more difficult that becomes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is a factor also making things more difficult the fact that the operational group is predominantly manned by volunteers and reservists?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, that's touching on what we were talking about yesterday, the difference between a fully professional army and an army that is made up of conscripts, reservists, part-timers, and et cetera. Yes, that does make his task more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is his task made additionally difficult also by the fact, if these soldiers, reservists, were called up for a military exercise and not for war, because, for instance, the state leadership had not declared a state of war?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, that's a command challenge. That's a morale issue. That's a moral and a morale issue, and the sort of challenge that commanders are trained and brought up to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: As for morale, they responded in terms of morale when they responded to a call-up. What I asked was whether reservists called up for a military exercise, and not for war, because the state leadership had not declared a state of war, is this an additional difficulty for the commander in his effort to create a command climate? Because he also has to deal with other matters pertaining to that particular fact.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. He's got to deal with the --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The witness has not been given a chance to fully finish his sentence, and he's entitled to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic. I think on this occasion I must rule with Ms. Somers. If the General is in a position to finish what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was going to say: Of course, he's got to deal with the issue as he finds it, and he will take the measures necessary to deal with the issue. Now, this is -- I don't pretend that this would not be a challenge. This would be a challenge. And this would -- this would be testing of his leadership. But that's what he's used to and that's what he's been trained for.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that the promotion of a firm military discipline, which is important for proper command, is also more difficult when units are formed from reservists and volunteers without sufficient previous training? Please be as brief as you can.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that, which is why it puts an additional responsibility on the commander in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: My question was: Would this make it more difficult to create a favourable command climate or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wouldn't necessarily make it easier or more difficult, but it would focus an area of attention where the commander had to place personal effort in order to create the command climate that he wanted to create.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that the implementation of the laws of war, under the circumstances previously described, is more difficult and a bigger problem than in the case of armies such as the British army, which have professional soldiers and regular composition of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I acknowledged that readily yesterday when I said that the difficulties involved in taking a rapidly put-together mobilised conscript force to war were difficult and that, therefore, the onus of responsibility on the commander to focus his attention on those areas which he thought most likely to go wrong was severe. In a perfect world, one goes to war with a fully trained organisation. The circumstances you're alluding to were the antithesis of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I will now put a few questions to you that have to do with the part of your report where you talk about the two up/two down command principle. My first question would be: What command doctrine, in your view, was preferred in the command system recommended in the reference materials you used?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command doctrine and two up/two down are not necessarily the same thing. I think we've already said that -- or I have already given an opinion that the command doctrine in place in the JNA was more the orders-driven doctrine rather than the mission-command-type doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that command in the JNA was centralised and implied an absence of initiative?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, I think we can agree on the first part, but I think the second part would probably be a slur on the JNA. When I've been talking about initiative, I've been talking about the use of initiative in order to achieve the objective within the higher commander's intent, not necessarily with orders at the time. I would not suggest that the JNA did not have initiative, but what I would suggest is that where they were using their initiative, it would be using it as a result of pretty specific orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can we then agree that decentralised command implies broad authority in the case of commanders and initiative at all levels of command?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can agree that, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So with reference to initiative, there is a difference in degree between centralised and decentralised command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In centralised command, subordinates will be expected to use their initiative in carrying out the specific orders they have been given. In decentralised command, the subordinate commanders will be expected to understand fundamentally the part they play in achieving the higher commander's intent and, where necessary, to act without orders if appropriate. There's a difference there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Will you please explain your understanding of the possibility of applying the two up/two down principle as a principle which is appropriate to decentralised command, in a fully centralised command system, such as that which existed in the former JNA. Please be brief, if you can.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think two up/two down will apply to the thought processes of most commanders in most armies. Two up is simply: Do I understand what I'm meant to be doing and why? Two down is a reality check on whether the tasks issued are within the resources available. I don't think they are necessarily dependent on specific forms of doctrine. They are actually applied common sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On page 9, at the end of your report, you quote a paragraph from a textbook on command and control from 1983, in order to support your thesis that, in the JNA command doctrine, one can find evidence for a two up/two down approach. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general terms, that is correct and is not surprising, because, as I said -- as I've just said, it is really applied common sense for what commanders need to do to carry out their function.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. To go back to this quotation, would you be so kind as to find the sentences which explicitly refer to a two up/two down approach.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my -- in the piece that I wrote, I've, at footnotes 14 and 17, I've quoted in the former a quotation taken out of a British command manual. And in the latter, a quotation taken out of rules for land -- for corps land forces from the SFRY's doctrine. And I've commented on the fact that, although they're not using the same words, they have a striking similarity. I'll read them out if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: No, thank you. I just wanted to hear what you've just said. Did you personally have an opportunity to analyse any of the command documents issued by the commander of the operational group?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in great detail, although I have seen a number of operational orders issued by the JNA, not necessarily by this operational group, and have been struck by the thoroughness of those orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Without going into a detailed analysis of particular command orders, is it not difficult to make conclusions about the two up/two down principle?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my conclusion is that JNA commanders were probably applying that thought process, like their colleagues in other armies apply that thought process, because it assists them in their planning and ordering process.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That is your assumption, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you asked me what conclusion I had drawn, and that is the conclusion that I have drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that even an implicit criticism of the commander for an operational group would require an analysis of a number of orders that he issued to his subordinates and reports that he submitted to his superiors?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one was to criticise the commander of an operational group on the basis of the orders that he had issued, then that would obviously require analysis in detail of those orders. Yes, I agree that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 10 of your report, you quoted a paragraph from a textbook on the role of the organ for operative teaching affairs. Can you tell me where in this paragraph you recognise the two up/two down principle?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Rodic. My report only goes to page 9. So what are we actually talking about? Are you talking about footnote 17? "The work of the corps command upon the receipt of an assignment comprises..."?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Footnote 16, the quotation connected to footnote 16.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Footnote 16, I have quoted. The quote reads: "The body for operative-educational affairs is responsible for the planning of operations and other forms of combat operations...It constantly monitors the situation, is familiar with the commander's decision..." That's looking up. "...the status of units of the corps..." That's looking down. "...the decisions of commanders of subordinated units...." That's looking down. "...the assignment of forces of other entities..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I will need to ask you to wind up in five minutes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have very important questions left. I had planned to cut short my cross-examination, but I still have important questions in relation to this principle, and the examination-in-chief went on for over three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, that's why I was giving you early warning, Mr. Rodic. Carry on quickly now, but we must allow some time to Ms. Somers for redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the operative educational affairs organ of the staff -- excuse me. That according to the command doctrine of the JNA, the operative educational organ was part of the staff in the narrow sense of the command of the unit, and that this organ planned operations and did not issue orders, and therefore, could not apply the two up/two down principle? Please reply briefly.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, anybody who is involved in planning that does not apply the two up/two down principle is planning in a vacuum.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the operative educational organ of the staff plans operations exclusively on the basis of the commander's decisions? The chief of staff, as his superior, tells him what those decisions are, and within the scope of activity of that organ, it is not possible to recognise the two up/two down principle.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The staff has a function in assisting the commander coming to his decision, and in that process, they would be, I would suggest, applying two up/two down, in order to be able to present to the commander various options on which the commander would make his decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the principle that was in force in the command doctrine of the JNA that tasks were assigned to immediately subordinated units and commanders and down the entire chain of command, every commander issued orders to commanding officers who were subordinated to him directly?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's no different, in my experience, to any chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, then, that in the command doctrine of the JNA, to which the reference materials relate that you rely on, are more appropriate to a one up/one down principle, rather than the one you prefer?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we can't agree that. I've explained two up/two down is more a thought process and a resources check mechanism, or that's what two down is. It's not an ordering mechanism. And two up is a mechanism to understand the part you play in the overall scheme of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I was asking you about the JNA and not the British army. From materials that you may not have studied when drawing up your report.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You're implying that two up/two down is the same as giving orders to the next level down. Everybody gives orders to the next level down. If you give orders to two levels down and skipping out the intermediate level, you're going to have a serious problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the paragraph before the last of your report, you quote from the army rules. That's footnote number 17. The rule corps of ground forces. On receipt of an assignment. Can you agree with me that this paragraph relates to, one, the duty of the commander to understand the goal of the operation or manoeuvre of his immediate superior, not superiors in the plural, as one might conclude on the basis of the context in which you quote this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think we can agree that, that specifically because it says: "The work of the corps commander upon receipt of an assignment comprises...studying and understanding the assignment..." That's what we would describe as mission analysis of the process, which I believe you also go through. "Understanding the assignment means grasping the objective of the action." That's in its widest context, I would suggest. The quotation continues: "The superior commander's idea of manoeuvre." This is your superior commander's idea of manoeuvre comes not just out of his head, but understanding the context in which he is giving his orders from what he is receiving from above. It goes on to say: "The place and the role of the corps within the framework of an assignment for several units, and the resulting tasks of the corps." That's -- and I have described it in terms of such. That, to me, reads very similarly to what the concept of working within a context of an understanding two up implies. That's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I would not agree with you, because this is in the singular. The commander's idea of manoeuvre. You quote this rule, but now you are speaking in the plural, going beyond this commander to an even higher level. This is very precise. It's put very precisely. The idea of the superior commander implies one up.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say the idea of the superior commander. It says: "The superior commander's idea of manoeuvre." His idea of manoeuvre is his plan of manoeuvre within the context within which he, the superior commander, is operating. So he's thinking above that. So to the guy we're talking about here, that's at least two up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I disagree with you on this issue. The rule is very precise.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps we'll agree to disagree, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Last couple of questions, Mr. Rodic, I think it must be.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When referring to the regulations, or rather, the instructions on the implementation of international laws of war in the SFRY, as one of the reference materials you give, do you know that this instruction and these regulations are implied -- are applied during an armed conflict in which the SFRY is participating, when the supreme command so orders and declares a state of war?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that. That is in the introduction to the document. The purpose of the rules of the international law of war is to prevent unnecessary casualties and suffering which do not significantly affect the military outcome of the war. It describes under what circumstances all this is to be applied and it talks about the responsibilities of commanders at all levels. If your question is a semantic one about was war declared or not, so be it. The actuality was there was a war in progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what rules and principles, what was the commander of the operational group to adhere to, was he to abide by? I mean the regulations then in force.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would expect him to abide by regulations in force, the conduct laid down by the JNA, standard operational procedures, international law, all that. I would expect him to abide by all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on your initiative, I will now end my cross-examination, although I still have a lot of material to go through. And may I suggest, because of this, the Defence tenders into evidence the entire documents, not just pages from these documents. Because tendering only pages is pulling out of context passages that are favourable to only one side. As the Prosecutor has these materials available, I suggest that they prepare them and hand them over. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, firstly, thank you for cooperating in the matter of time. Some very important matters have been dealt with and the Chamber has benefitted in particular from the early part of your cross-examination today. Ms. Somers, I think it would be appropriate, not necessarily now, but when you've gathered the materials, if the whole document were to be tendered, in the circumstances, and if you would like now to re-examine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may in due course handle the tendering issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: General Pringle, can you please clarify whether it is within a commander's duty to act, one way or the other, when he becomes aware, and this is for the sake of argument, that a mentally unstable battalion commander who is in charge of weaponry and other human beings, and the fate of civilians, is in his area of responsibility, and that in fact, a negative consequence has resulted from his action, based perhaps on a number of factors, but his action?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would comment under those circumstances that it is the immediate responsibility of the next level of commander to act, and it is the responsibility of the levels of command above that to ensure that action is taken. To have a mentally unstable battalion commander in charge of weaponry left in place carries very obvious implications, and therefore, there is a clear responsibility on the command chain to take the necessary action.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier, General, that the higher up, perhaps the more difficult it is to deal with lower-level matters; however, you indicated that it was still part of command, albeit difficult. If the incidents or the difficulties that are associated with the actions by an individual at the battalion commander level who is alleged, and I say only alleged, to have mentally unstable -- to be mentally unstable, if these incidents are of such notoriety as to invoke response from the international community, as well as the other side bringing it to the attention - and by "international community," I would say international monitors and international media - then would this be sufficient notice, or at least would the duty to act be triggered?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say under those circumstances that we're almost past the stage where the duty to act has become apparent. Under the circumstances you've painted, I would judge that it is plainly obvious that action should have already been taken, let alone needs to be taken now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would this be so even if at the top -- even if the top or the formation involved is an ad hoc formation? Does that really matter?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether the top formation is ad hoc or not, it still has a commander, and a commander has authority vested in him as the commander to ensure that the necessary actions are being taken at the necessary level.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You were asked on cross-examination as to what would be the -- whether or not the matter would be closed as to an investigation into the behaviour we have just discussed in the hypothetical, if a corps commander had been dealing with -- or had been dealt with directly by someone at the level of Ministry of Defence, or in that very high federal level, bypassing the operational group or the higher commander in the interim. I want to understand your comment. Are you suggesting that - in this instance, you referred to 2nd Operational Group commander, can selectively, willing abrogate his authority as to certain issues and invoke it as to others? What would happen if that were the case?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic and I had a lengthy discussion on this, rather based around that uncertainty. I do find the hypothesis suggested that the top of the operational chain of command has been bypassed and that the Ministry of Defence is dealing over the head of that commander down to the corps commander. And in so doing, the hypothesis was that the operational level group commander had declared himself satisfied with that and had effectively, therefore, abrogated his responsibility. I said many times over that I found that to be -- I think the word I used was irregular, and I could only repeat it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If, in fact, the commander at the 2nd Operational Group level was unhappy --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers is speaking of the commander of the 2nd Operational Group. This is precisely what Your Honour drew attention to several times. The witness is to explain general principles. The last two questions are specific. They are not hypothetical, as if Mr. Pringle could say something about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Petrovic, you misunderstand Ms. Somers's reference to 2nd Operational Group. She was speaking in her hypothesis of two distinct operational groups, the first and the second, not a particular unit of the JNA army. That is the way I understood it. Is that what you meant, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm more than happy not even to put a number there. My point was it was raised in cross-examination with that very specific title, and I'm only taking from what was raised in cross-examination. But I'm happy to say if the head of an operational group --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Please. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If the head of an operational group that was over a corps commander is unhappy with a -- either interference by or bypassing by or the result of an order given by his superior commanders at the higher level, discussed in our previous hypothetical, according to what you said earlier, or yesterday, perhaps, then he would, rather than disobey it, have to question that order, would he not; and if he did not agree, then what would he do?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that. Indeed, I think I said pretty well that. I said that the operational group commander in question would, at the very least, query with the Ministry of Defence why he's being bypassed. And I can envisage very little circumstances where a commander would agree to him being bypassed in the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But if bypassed and finds out about a result with which he is not happy because he perhaps, as you said, is responsible for everything in his area of responsibility, including the retention of someone who has been deemed mentally unstable, then if he's unhappy, what would he do about that unhappiness?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then he has a duty to say something about it, because the retention of this mentally defective, or however we are describing him, commander, in his operational area of responsibility is going to have implications for him. This would not be a minor matter. If an operational commander is being told, for whatever reasons, that the Ministry of Defence is quite happy that he has a mentally defective battalion commander in his command and he is not to remove him, then that operational commander, I would suggest, would be vociferous in his objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If, for the sake of argument, the offending conduct, perhaps, in a legal attack was directed by or ordered by a mentally unstable officer or commander, but not necessarily the result of his mental instability, would the fact of the breach of order nevertheless cause the superior commanders to take action?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The superior commanders would be required to take action on the breach of orders, at all levels.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you be able to offer your view on whether or not a person, a commander who has been heading a battalion, let's say during the time period we were discussing, is permitted to remain in the military for some -- more than five years afterward and is promoted, would there be any inference drawn about, (a), his ability to perform in the military; and (b), the general attitude toward orders being implemented?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he's not only allowed to remain in the army but is also promoted, then there is, in my opinion, a very direct inference that his actions are condoned, indeed approved of, and worthy of promotion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If the operations group commander, operational group commander, who may be very unhappy but is forced or is nevertheless left in a position where he allows the offending or allegedly offending battalion commander to remain in place, and this operational group commander remains in the military for several years afterward and also is awarded a promotion, does that suggest that either the unhappiness passed or that he elected not to choose any other options to protest?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, may I say that suggests to me more a study in personal behaviour than in military principles.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I can cut right to the heart of the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If the operations commander, operational commander, disagreed strongly enough, would you expect a resignation or some action along that line, rather than leaving a problem under his control?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the operational commander felt sufficiently strongly enough about being forced to retain in his chain of command somebody who was mentally unstable, I would expect at least a very formal objection to the appropriate level, the Ministry of Defence, possibly -- and leading to possibly a resignation. I would also expect a clear explanation that he would not be held responsible for the unstable commander if he was forced to retain him. He would find himself in a horrendously difficult position, and under many circumstances, many commanders would say, "I cannot execute command and take responsibility that everything happens in my command if this is what I'm being forced to deal with," and would take the necessary actions, such as resignation, as a result.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions. Thank you, Your Honours, for indulging me the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Somers. We're grateful to counsel with their assistance with time today. May I thank you for your attendance, General, and the assistance that you've given us. And you are now free to go as you will.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The hearing will continue on Tuesday of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 3rd day of February, 2004.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.57 p.m.,
